summary: The pilot is legally responsible for weight, balance and performance. Overloading lengthens take-off and landing, cuts climb and range, and raises stall speed. A forward CG raises stall speed, an aft CG reduces pitch stability. CG is total moment divided by total weight. AFM performance is unfactored, so GA pilots should apply safety factors (take-off x1.33, landing x1.43). Built from CAA Safety Sense Leaflet 9.
src: Safety Sense Leaflet 9: Weight, Balance and Performance
sections: Responsibility and empty weight
The pilot in command must keep the aircraft within weight and balance limits for the whole flight, and confirm it can take off, climb and land in the space available
Use the schedule for your own airframe, not a generic type schedule
Basic empty weight normally includes oil, unusable fuel and fitted equipment
If you might exceed MTOW, find real passenger and baggage weights (include lifejackets, coats and bags). Check baggage compartment and seat limits
Fuel weight
Check tank quantities against the schedule with a dipstick, because gauges can be wrong
For weight and balance assume fuel is on the high side, for fuel planning assume low
AVGAS is about 0.72 kg/L, Jet A-1 about 0.8 kg/L. MOGAS varies, so weigh a litre
Effects of overloading
Longer take-off run and higher take-off speed
Reduced acceleration, climb angle, climb rate and ceiling
Reduced range and poorer controllability
Higher stall and landing speeds, longer landing roll and reduced braking
Smaller structural margins, and performance beyond limits cannot be predicted
Balance and the centre of gravity
Datum is the reference point. Arm is distance from datum. Moment = weight x arm
CG = total moments / total weight
Forward CG: higher stall speed, heavier nose, less nose-up authority, more drag and fuel burn
Aft CG: hard to trim, less pitch stability, pitch-up at low speed and high power, degraded stall and unknown spin behaviour
CG can move as fuel burns, so calculate for take-off and landing
Heavy small items (tool box) matter. Load evenly side to side and respect fuel imbalance limits
Worked CG example
Empty 700 kg at 2.22 m = 1,554. Front seats 160 kg at 2.05 m = 328. Rear seats 70 kg at 2.98 m = 208.6
Baggage 15 kg at 3.63 m = 54.45. Fuel 100 kg at 2.41 m = 241
Total weight 1,045 kg, total moment 2,386.05
CG = 2,386.05 / 1,045 = 2.28 m aft of datum, then check it sits inside the envelope limits
Performance principles and definitions
AFM figures are unfactored: a new aircraft, a proficient pilot, no wear
Take-off distance includes climb to 50 ft. Landing distance is measured from crossing the threshold at 50 ft
TORA take-off run available. TODA = TORA plus clearway. ASDA = TORA plus stopway. LDA landing distance available
Standard reference is 1013 hPa and 15°C. Pressure altitude is the altimeter reading with 1013 set. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature
Rule of thumb: 30 ft per hPa (the leaflet gives the more precise 27 ft)
Rule-of-thumb multipliers
+10% weight: take-off x1.2, landing x1.1
+1,000 ft elevation: take-off x1.1, landing x1.05
+10°C temperature: take-off x1.1, landing x1.05
Tailwind of 10% of lift-off speed: x1.2 for both
2% uphill slope: take-off x1.1. 2% downhill slope: landing x1.1
Multiply multiple factors together
Safety factors
Dry grass: take-off x1.2, landing x1.15
Wet grass: take-off x1.3, landing x1.35
Wet paved surface: landing x1.15
Soft ground or snow: x1.25 both
General factor applied last: take-off x1.33, landing x1.43
Do not operate if factored distances exceed those available
Rejected take-off and climb
Pick a visual decision point where you will abort if not enough speed. Move it earlier if the full ASDA is not available
Reasons to reject before the decision point: abnormal engine, poor acceleration, losing the centreline, bird strike, open door, loss of airspeed
After the decision point, minor problems are handled in the air. Never force a lift-off below rotation speed
Minimum climb rates: single-engine 500 ft/min, multi-engine with one engine out 150 ft/min
Required rate of climb = (ground speed / 60) x gradient in ft per NM. Example: 500 ft in 2 NM is 250 ft/NM. At 70 kt that needs about 291 ft/min
Non-turbo piston aircraft lose a lot of climb above 5,000 ft density altitude
Units and conversions
1 kg = 2.205 lb. 1 ft = 0.305 m. 1 Imperial gal = 4.546 L. 1 US gal = 3.785 L
1 Imperial gal = 1.205 US gal
Mixed units have caused accidents: check every document and match the specific gravity to the volume unit

Which statement about AFM performance figures is correct?
o: They are unfactored, for a new aircraft and a proficient pilot
They already include safety margins for an average pilot
They apply only to paved runways, so grass needs no factor
They ignore weight, so the figures suit any loading
quiz.why: AFM data is unfactored, so GA pilots should add their own safety factors.
